The VELYS robotic-assisted solution

A strategic technology evaluation informed through scoping review

S R Morrison, A J Hall, N D Clement, C Gee, S Chopra, J V Clarke

This review article was published in Computer Assisted Surgery and is freely available to read and download in full under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. It evaluates a single robotic platform against the research priorities set by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in its 2025 early value assessment of robot-assisted surgery for orthopaedic procedures.

Abstract

Robot-assisted surgery (RAS) is increasingly utilized in arthroplasty, with emerging evidence suggesting potential benefits, however, the overall evidence base remains immature. Given the heterogeneity of available systems, device-specific evaluation is required. The VELYS Robotic-Assisted Solution (VRAS; Johnson & Johnson MedTech) is an imageless, semi-active robotic platform for knee arthroplasty. This study provides a structured strategic evaluation of VRAS aligned with the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence Early Value Assessment (EVA) and proposes a roadmap for future evidence generation. 16 relevant studies were identified in a systematic literature search, predominantly retrospective and lacking randomized controlled trials. Findings were synthesized using a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats framework, with subsequent analysis to inform strategic recommendations. Key strengths of VRAS include avoidance of pre-operative computed tomography imaging, integration with established implant systems, a relatively short learning curve, and early signals of improved short-term outcomes. Weaknesses center on the limited quality and maturity of the evidence base, absence of long-term outcome data, and system-specific design considerations such as lack of haptic feedback boundaries. Opportunities include reduced resource burden with imageless workflows and potential optimization of patient outcomes, while threats involve high capital costs, competition from more established RAS platforms, and the risk of unmet evidence requirements within defined timelines. Across EVA domains, evidence for patient-reported outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and long-term clinical benefit remains insufficient. High-quality, adequately powered studies, comprehensive health-economic analyses, and registry-linked longitudinal studies are essential to define the clinical and economic value of VRAS in light of the EVA.

Background · The System and the Early Value Assessment

Robotic systems differ enough to need evaluating one at a time

In April 2025 NICE published research priorities for six robot-assisted knee arthroplasty systems as an early value assessment, establishing a three-year evidence-generation period after which decisions on adoption or further evaluation will be made. The assessment asks for evidence on health-related quality of life, resource use including economic modelling, post-surgery outcomes and service use, and outcomes in different patient subgroups.

Because these systems differ in design philosophy, mechanics and service requirements, including whether preoperative computed tomography (CT) is needed, the authors set out to evaluate one system in depth against the assessment rather than treat robot-assisted surgery as a single technology. The VELYS Robotic-Assisted Solution is an imageless, table-mounted, semi-active system in which a robotic arm guides bone cuts with a tracked saw, using infrared trackers in the femur and tibia, and it uses the established ATTUNE knee implant. Among the six systems, it is the only semi-active imageless system that cuts directly through a robotic arm.

Results · Evidence Against the EVA Priorities

Most of the evidence concerns efficiency, and very little concerns patients

Of 25 reports assessed in full, 16 were included: 13 retrospective studies (81.2%), including cohort, comparative and registry analyses, and three prospective cohort studies, with no randomised controlled trials or systematic reviews. Studies of accuracy and safety alone were excluded by design, since the assessment already accepts these systems as safe and more accurate than manual techniques, as were studies using computer-assisted navigation as the comparator. Only two of the included studies were used by NICE as key evidence and four more were noted, so ten had not been considered by the assessment.

EVA evidence areaStudiesWhat the VELYS literature shows
Health-related quality of life and PROMs7Early signals in small cohorts: better Forgotten Joint Score and pain than manual surgery in one study (significant at 12 weeks only), better Knee Society Function Scores in another, improvement from baseline in patients with severe extra-articular deformity in a third, and no significant difference from manual surgery in the remaining four.
Consumables and resourcing10The best-evidenced area: learning curves are short and operative times approach those of manual surgery, although comparative studies reported VELYS adding from about four to 23 minutes of theatre time. Two US propensity-matched studies found a higher 90-day care cost than manual surgery ($15,357 vs $14,944) but a lower cost than other robotic systems as a group ($15,048 vs $16,867).
Post-surgery treatment and service use4Shorter length of stay and fewer 90-day hospital revisits in retrospective and registry-based studies, with similar 90-day revision rates.
Population subgroups–Demographics are reported, but there is little subgroup analysis from which to draw conclusions about specific patient populations.

Results · Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats

Distinct design strengths, set against an immature evidence base

Strengths
  • No preoperative imaging required
  • Real-time feedback and precision
  • Compact design with a small theatre footprint
  • Direct cutting, giving better surgical control
  • Integrated with well-evidenced, familiar implants
  • Non-inferior or improved efficiency
Weaknesses
  • Less evidence than competing systems
  • Lack of long-term outcome data
  • No force-feedback haptic boundary
  • Single-company implant lock
  • Service-level learning curve and initial cost
Opportunities
  • Demand gives an opportunity to improve knee arthroplasty
  • Potential to improve satisfaction, clinical outcomes and revision rates
  • May serve higher-risk patients safely and effectively
  • Less reliance on over-burdened radiology services
  • Regulatory support for real-world data collection
Threats
  • High initial cost may be prohibitive
  • Competition from systems with broader evidence bases
  • Risk of inequitable access between centres
  • NICE support may be withdrawn if real-world data are insufficient
  • Implant lock-in could limit flexibility

Condensed from Table 2 of the paper. The SWOT matrix was mapped to a TOWS analysis, which pairs internal and external factors to generate strategies, for example using the imageless workflow to support economic and efficiency assessment, and prioritising early publication of evidence within the assessment window.

Infographic

SWOT findings, evidence gaps and research recommendations

Research Priorities & Limitations

What the evidence needs within the three-year window

01
Adequately powered randomised trials against manual arthroplasty
Trials should use patient-relevant outcome measures with defined minimal clinically important differences, avoid instruments with ceiling effects, build subgroup analysis into their power calculations, and assess total and unicompartmental procedures separately.
02
Registry coding by system and implant
Joint registries should record which robotic system and implant combination was used, so that revision rates can be compared per system rather than per manufacturer implant, with follow-up of at least ten years.
03
Comprehensive economic evaluation
Micro-costing, theatre throughput, staffing and procedures per day are needed, alongside quality-adjusted life years, since current cost data come from the United States and exclude the capital cost of the robot.
04
Team workload and learning
Training needs and workload for the wider theatre team are unassessed; tools such as the NASA Task Load Index, highlighted in the assessment, could measure them at intervals as teams gain experience.
Limitations: the VELYS evidence base is immature and predominantly retrospective, some included studies carry conflicts of interest related to the system, heterogeneity in design, outcome measures and follow-up limits comparison between studies and between systems, and the reliance on expert opinion within the SWOT and TOWS framework introduces an element of subjectivity. No formal risk of bias assessment was undertaken.

Take-Home Messages

Robot-assisted arthroplasty systems are heterogeneous technologies that require system-specific evaluation rather than collective appraisal, particularly within the NICE early value assessment.
The VELYS system has distinct design and implementation strengths, including an imageless workflow, established implants and a relatively short learning curve, but its evidence base remains comparatively immature.
Evidence for patient-reported outcomes, cost-effectiveness and long-term clinical benefit is insufficient for VELYS, as it is to varying degrees for the other systems in the assessment.
Coordinated multicentre research, including adequately powered randomised trials, registry-linked longitudinal studies and full economic evaluation, will be needed to define the clinical and economic value of the system.

Our Related Articles

Related SCOTTISH Network research

This evaluation belongs to a programme of SCOTTISH Network work on robot-assisted knee arthroplasty, which includes a full scoping review of the VELYS literature and a review of how patients and the public perceive robotic surgery.

Scoping Review · Robotic Knee Arthroplasty
Use of the VELYS Robotic-Assisted Solution in knee arthroplasty: a scoping review
Morrison SR, Hall AJ, Clement ND, Walmsley PJ, Gee C, Clarke JV · Journal of Experimental Orthopaedics · 2026;13(2):e70726 · doi:10.1002/jeo2.70726
The companion scoping review covers the wider VELYS literature, including the accuracy and safety studies set aside in the present evaluation. Across 25 studies, VELYS improved implant positioning accuracy with a non-inferior early safety profile, while claims of improved patient outcomes, function and efficiency were not well evidenced in a largely retrospective literature without randomised controlled trials.
View study page Read in JEO ↗
Scoping Review · Patient & Public Perception
Perceptions of robot-assisted arthroplasty among patients and the public
Morrison SR, Clement ND, Clarke JV, Gee C, Chopra S, Hall AJ · Bone & Joint Open · 2026;7(6):733–743 · doi:10.1302/2633-1462.76.BJO-2026-0007.R1
High patient interest is one of the strengths identified in the present evaluation. This scoping review of 16 studies and 3,957 participants found that patients showed high interest in robot-assisted surgery but commonly overestimated its benefits and how widely it is used, and that trust in the operating surgeon remained a stronger influence than the technology itself.
